newsitem.title: THAILAND: FEATURE - Thai 1997 commodities exports set to grow.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Thai 1997 commodities exports set to grow.

text.p: The export outlook for Thailand's agricultural commodities in 1997 remain reasonably bright in terms of volume but it may be soft on value.
Latest commerce ministry data project a 1.4 percent growth for agricultural exports next year on the back of an expected improvement in the global economy.

The exports are expected to earn 214.9 billion baht ($8.59 billion) in foreign exchange, accounting for 13.6 percent of total exports for Thailand, a major commodities exporter, according to the data.
High production costs were likely to remain a problem and would affect the competitiveness of Thai commodities, mostly for rice and rubber.
But overall, Thailand is likely to remain a leading world exporter of rice, tapioca, rubber and sugar next year, analysts told Reuters.
WORLD'S BIGGEST RICE EXPORTER

Thailand's status as the world's biggest rice exporter is set to remain intact. The government set the export target for 1997 at five million tonnes compared with 5.2 million tonnes projected for 1996.
"Next year will continue to be golden year for Thai rice. But the gold might not fetch as much cash as it used to," said Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee.
His ministry attributed the bullish outlook to a possible drop in exports from India because of floods and a delayed harvest in Vietnam.

However, Pracha Charutrakulchai, head of the commerce ministry's foreign trade department, said rising Thai production costs would erode its competitiveness against low cost producers India and Vietnam.
High quality rice, which made up about 40 percent of total exports, will see another good year, while medium and lower grade rice could face a tougher time, analysts said.
The agriculture ministry has forecast that 1996/97 (April-March) rice production would drop to 21.26 million tonnes from 22.01 million in the previous season.
SUGAR OUTLOOK NOT SWEET

For sugar, the outlook will not be exceptionally sweet next year. Industry sources said export volume would continue to be strong, but prices would be pressured by expected increases in global supply.
Thailand's sugar exports for the 1996/97 season (November-October) could reach 4.6 million tonnes compared with 4.38 million tonnes estimated for 1995/96.
It expected to produce 6.28 million tonnes of sugar next year while domestic consumption was estimated at 1.7 million tonnes.

"We won't have any problem selling. However, with the news of surpluses everywhere, prices are not likely to be very good," said Sukhum Vicheanratanapong, deputy general manager of the Thai Cane and Sugar Corp.
The International Sugar Organisation has forecast that the sugar surplus for the 1996/97 season should total 2.87 million tonnes raw value.
Many traders expected activity in the market to be moderate until China enters the scene again, probably by the second quarter of 1997.

Despite news of surpluses, some traders said they were still optimistic. "It might not be that bad. First of all, the surplus this season is sharply reduced from last season's which was seen at almost six million tonnes," said a trader from one Japanese trading house.
"Secondly, will all this surplus translate into total availability? Besides, it all depends on the weather. There could be a crop failure anywhere between now and the end of the season."
RUBBER EXPORTS TO REMAIN STRONG

The volume of exports of Thai natural rubber next year was likely to remain robust and projected to be around the level hit in 1996, but export value was expected to increase marginally, industry and official sources said.
Thailand, the world's top producer and exporter of natural rubber since 1991, is expected to export 1.6 million tonnes from 1.88 million tonnes in 1996.

The International Rubber Study Group forecast that 1997 world natural rubber consumption was set to rise at a steady rate of 3.8 percent over 1996 to 6.34 million tonnes, but the output would total only 6.24 million tonnes.

The Dutch agri-bank Rabobank said in a recent report that continued growth in Asian countries, especially China, Taiwan, South Korea and other newly-industrialised countries, would support demand for Thai rubber.
However, high production costs, especially for tapping rubber, could threaten Thailand's premier position in the world natural rubber market, industry sources said.

"The country's supremacy on the world rubber market will come under increasing threat from Indonesia in the next few years unless steps are taken to boost productivity and cut relatively high costs of rubber tapping," the Rabobank report said.
The Thai government plans to encourage more production of value-added rubber such as technically specified rubber (TSR) and increase domestic rubber-based manufacturing.

"We can't go on exporting sheet rubbers alone and must move upmarket. Otherwise, we will be beaten by lower-cost producer such as Indonesia," said Sucharit Promdej, head of the Rubber Research Institute.
TAPIOCA PRICES UNDER PRESSURE
Grain surpluses in the European Union, Thailand's single biggest outlet for tapioca, looked set to pressure prices of exports in 1997, industry sources said.

"The demand is still there...But exports are likely to fetch less money. We have to compete with other feed ingredients such as wheat, barley and other grains," said Seri Denworalak, head of the Thai Tapioca Trade Association.
The commerce ministry estimated the EU would produce bumper crops of about 204 million tonnes of grain in the 1996/97 crop year, up from 175 million tonnes previously.
